items.title: Women pay to break things
items.text: Across the UK, a growing number of people, especially women, are turning to so-called rage rooms to destroy everyday items like flat-screen televisions and crockery with mallets and hammers. Owners report that up to three-quarters of their customers are female. Many use the sessions to cope with everyday stress, child-rearing pressures, or deep emotional trauma such as bereavement . Psychologists note that societal expectations often force women to suppress anger, unlike sports events where men are traditionally permitted to shout freely. Inside a rage room, participants find a safe, controlled environment where they can express frustration without judgment . While smashing objects provides an immediate surge of adrenaline and physical relief, experts caution that it doesn’t serve as a permanent therapeutic cure for long-term psychological problems. Instead, they view it as a helpful short-term release of energy, and advise individuals dealing with deep-seated emotional pain to seek professional long-term support. Difficult words: bereavement (suffering the loss of a loved one through death), suppress (to forcibly hold back, control, or prevent the expression of a feeling), judgment (an opinion or decision formed after thought or legal process). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

items.title: Women pay to break things
items.text: Rage rooms are becoming very popular in the UK, especially for women. In these special rooms, people pay to break things like old TVs, plates, and glasses with big hammers. About 75 percent of the customers are women who are trying to deal with work stress, busy family lives, or deep sadness after losing loved ones. Experts explain that society usually expects women to stay calm, so they don’t have many places to express anger. Smashing things gives people a quick feeling of power and release. On the other hand, doctors say that while rage rooms are fun and help you feel better for a short time, breaking things doesn’t fix big emotional problems forever. Difficult words: rage (uncontrollable anger), sadness (when you are sad), smash (to break something into pieces with great force). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Women pay to break things
items.text: Many women in the UK are visiting new places called rage room s. In these rooms, people use hammers to break old TVs, plates, and boxes. People go there because they feel very stressed , tired, or sad about life and work. Owners of these rooms say that most of their visitors are women. Doctors say that it is good to let out bad feelings in a safe space. Men can get angry during sports, but women must be quiet and calm. Breaking things makes people feel happy and strong for a short time. But it cannot solve big life problems forever. Difficult words: hammer (a hand tool which we use for breaking things), stressed (worried and upset), owner (a person who has something and it belongs to him or her). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Are squishy toys safe?
items.text: Squishy toys have become extremely popular among children, who collect and squeeze them for stress relief. However, international safety concerns have prompted investigations into what these toys contain. Researchers and journalists tested 18 different squishies in Singapore for harmful chemicals like benzene and phthalates that are linked to cancer, hormone disruption , and developmental risks. While no benzene was detected, laboratory testing revealed that several toys contained restricted plasticisers . One pink toy exceeded Singapore’s legal limit by 1.7 times. Experts warn that prolonged heat, such as being left inside a parked car, can cause these toys to soften, leak, or rupture under pressure, and potentially cause skin irritation or burns. Following the findings, the affected retailer pulled the unsafe product from its shelves and offered customers refunds. Authorities advise parents to inspect toy labels carefully, avoid leaving them in direct sunlight, and monitor children during play. Difficult words: phthalate (a chemical additive that makes plastics softer, more flexible, and resilient), hormone disruption (an interference with the hormones, which can affect growth and health), plasticiser (a chemical substance added to materials to increase their softness, flexibility, or stretchiness). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

items.title: Are squishy toys safe?
items.text: Squishy toys are very popular with children who love to collect and squeeze them. But reports from around the world show that some of these toys may not be safe. A team in Singapore tested 18 squishy toys in a laboratory to check for dangerous chemicals. They found that most toys were fine, but one pink toy had high levels of a chemical called DINP, which is used to make plastic soft. This chemical was higher than local safety limits and can be harmful to children’s health. Tests also showed that if squishies are left in a hot car, they can get very hot, break, and leak dangerous liquid. After finding these results, the store removed the unsafe toy and offered refunds to customers. Difficult words: squishy (a soft toy), safety limit (the maximum amount of a chemical in a product to be still safe), refund (money given back to a customer who returns an unsafe or unwanted product). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Are squishy toys safe?
items.text: Many kids love playing with squishy toys. Scientists test some of these toys to see if they are safe. They find that one toy has too much of one chemical. This chemical can hurt children. Also, if squishies stay in a hot car for a long time, they can break. Hot liquid may come out. This can hurt a child’s skin. The store takes the bad toy away. They give money back to parents. Experts tell families to check toy labels and keep the toys away from hot places like cars. Difficult words: squishy (soft, not hard when you touch it), liquid (a substance which flows, like water or gel), label (a piece of paper on a product which gives information about it). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Wire upgrade at fault for grounding all US flights
items.text: Thousands of flights across the USA were grounded on Friday the 13th following a major communications failure in the country's air traffic control system. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ordered a nationwide ground stop after problems with radar and communications equipment. More than 3,500 airplanes were in the air at the time. Thousands of flights were cancelled, leaving passengers stranded at airports nationwide. The problem was eventually traced to an overloaded router, possibly as a result of maintenance work to replace decades-old copper wires with fibre-optic cables. The FAA lifted the ground stop almost five hours later. Operations may take days to return to normal. The incident sparked widespread concern. Officials quickly reassured the public that it was not another 9/11. The US homeland security secretary said there had been no indication of a cyberattack or national security threat. He described the incident as a "telecommunications outage". Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed the failure on outdated infrastructure. He said: "We have old switches and old routers. We use 1980s little copper lines." He added: "It's an old system that went down. It went down everywhere. It got overloaded." Duffy warned that systems would "continue to break" unless Congress allocated extra funds. He said: "I can't build things if I don't have money." items.title: France blames Iran for cyberattack on freezers
items.text: The French government has blamed Iran for a cyberattack on supermarket freezers and refrigerators across France. The attacks happened last month. They hit around 700 supermarkets and shops. Hackers took control of the cooling systems in the fridges and freezers. Temperatures increased to more than 50 degrees Celsius. Thousands of tons of frozen food melted. Stores had to throw the food away because it was no longer safe to eat. The French Foreign Minister said the attack was on a level never seen before. France believes an Iranian cyber unit carried out the attack. Iran has strongly denied it was involved in the attacks and blamed the French government for them. Security experts have warned that cyberattacks could be more dangerous in the future. Similar attacks have already affected other European countries. A French blood bank has also been hit. Fortunately, workers stopped the blood products from being damaged. Cybersecurity expert Gerome Billois stated: "At the moment, they are attacking easy equipment, but we should be prepared to see attacks on other systems like water or electricity." Weak computer security can let hackers attack places and services, such as hospitals, airports, public transport and banks. This can put people's lives in danger. items.title: Chef fired for refusing to put pineapple on pizza
items.text: An Italian chef in Brisbane, Australia, has been fired for refusing to put pineapple on pizzas, among other reasons. He went to the Fair Work Commission to fight his dismissal, but failed to get his job back. The chef stated that topping pizzas with the tropical fruit was an "insult to his culture". He claimed he was sacked from a restaurant in May after repeatedly refusing his boss's instructions to make pineapple and ham pizzas for diners. His employer contended that the refusal was one of several workplace issues. The commission rejected the chef's application because it was submitted after the deadline. The chef has since found a job at another Italian restaurant. The question of whether pineapple belongs on pizza is a controversial one. It continues to divide public opinion. Pizza purists are aghast at the idea, but it is an established menu staple in many countries. The Hawaiian pizza was reportedly invented in Canada in 1962 after a chef used ham and pineapple as toppings. The restaurant owner expressed his opinion on it. He admitted that while the pizza was not his "absolute favourite," he would not "turn his nose up at it". Many restaurateurs insist that customers should be free to enjoy whatever ingredients and toppings they choose. items.title: Man completes 28-year walk around the world
items.text: A British man has completed an amazing 28-year walk around the world. Former soldier Karl Bushby, 57, arrived home in the city of Hull in England on Monday. He started his adventure in November 1998 in Chile, South America. His plan was to walk all the way home without using cars, boats, buses, trains, or airplanes. During his journey, he travelled about 58,000 kilometres through 29 countries. He crossed frozen seas, deserts, mountains, and jungles. He also faced many dangers. These included encountering polar bears and kidnappers, and spending time in a Russian prison. His journey was expected to take 12 years. However, problems with money, visas, and borders made his trip a lot longer. Thousands of people welcomed Mr Bushby home. He was very happy to finally finish his journey. His mother was waiting outside his childhood home to greet him. Bushby joked: "Sorry to keep you waiting." He also told the cheering crowd that many people around the world had helped him get home. He said he could not have done it alone. Britain's Prime Minister congratulated him on his achievement. He praised Bushby's determination and belief in himself. Bushby told the Guardian newspaper that he wasn't so interested in walking. He said: "It's boring as hell." That didn't stop him walking across four continents. items.title: Trump loses control of Congress
items.text: Following a decisive defeat in the US midterm elections, Donald Trump and the Republican Party have lost control of both houses of Congress to the Democrats. The results have sparked intense disputes within both major parties. Among Republicans, Vice President JD Vance has attributed the electoral losses to the unpopular war with Iran, which created a visible rift with the president. At the same time, Donald Trump has sent mixed signals regarding his policy direction: while publicly acknowledging that his strict immigration enforcement went too far, he appointed Stephen Miller, the architect of those policies, as White House Chief of Staff. On the Democratic side, progressives and moderates are competing to shape the party’s future legislative agenda. Political analysts warn that despite the significant shift in congressional control, deep ideological divisions and the president’s veto power will likely lead to continued political gridlock in Washington rather than major policy changes. Difficult words: dispute (a disagreement, argument, or debate between people, parties, or groups), rift (a serious break in friendly relations between people or groups), gridlock (a situation where no progress can be made because of strong disagreement or opposing forces). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

items.title: Trump loses control of Congress
items.text: The Democratic Party won big in the US midterm elections and took control of both houses of Congress from President Donald Trump’s Republican Party. This defeat caused strong arguments inside both parties. Vice President JD Vance blamed the election loss on the war with Iran, and disagreed directly with Trump. At the same time, Trump said his strict immigration rules went too far, but he still chose the creator of those rules to lead his White House team. Meanwhile, Democrats are fighting over their plans, as its members want different things. Experts say that even with new Democratic leaders in Congress, it will be hard to pass major new laws because the president can still block them, which may lead to more political delays in Washington. Difficult words: defeat (the loss of a contest, game, election, or battle), blame (to say or think that someone or something is responsible for something bad that happened), major (important, big, serious). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Trump loses control of Congress
items.text: The Democrats win a big election in the US. They now control Congress. President Donald Trump and his team lose many votes . Now, people in both political parties are fighting about what to do next. Vice President JD Vance says that the war with Iran is a bad idea. Many people do not like Trump anymore because of that. Trump said that his immigration rules are too hard. But he still puts his immigration leader in a top job. At the same time, Democrats are trying to agree on new plans for the country. Experts think that it will still be very hard for leaders in Washington to pass new laws and help people quickly. Difficult words: vote (when a person formally chooses a person in an election), immigration rules (what people who come from other countries must and must not do), pass (to officially say yes to a new rule). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Study finds majority of pilots nod off mid-flight
items.text: A new report has raised serious concerns about pilot fatigue. The European Cockpit Association (ECA) conducted a survey of nearly 7,200 pilots across 32 countries. It discovered that exhaustion in the cockpit is a widespread and underreported problem. More than three-quarters of respondents said they had briefly dozed off while operating an aircraft in the month before the survey. Almost a quarter of them admitted they continued flying even when they were too tired. Furthermore, half said they had operated a flight when they should have declared themselves unfit for duty. Tiredness can result from long working hours, insufficient rest, and unpredictable schedules. The pilots were very frank in their answers to the survey questions. Many said they were reluctant to report fatigue because they feared punishment or other negative reactions from their bosses. Captain Coen George, a director of the ECA, warned: "When pilots fear career consequences, fatigue goes unreported and the risk returns to the cockpit." Aviation safety experts say exhaustion can impair judgement, slow reaction times and prevent pilots from responding effectively to unexpected in-flight situations. The experts urged airlines to foster a culture in which pilots can report tiredness without fear of repercussions. Carriers should ensure that passenger safety is their top priority. items.title: Pope Leo visits South America
items.text: Pope Leo drew a crowd of one million people at a nighttime vigil in Buenos Aires on Tuesday during his 12-day South American tour. The pontiff addressed the gathered youth, urged them not to be consumed by the pursuit of wealth, physical appearance, or social media popularity, and warned against humiliating others online. This event followed an outdoor Mass in Cordoba earlier that day, which attracted 650,000 attendees, and a record-breaking gathering of 2.5 million people in Buenos Aires on Monday. As the first pope to visit Catholic-majority Argentina since 1987, Leo seeks to revitalize the Church’s presence in the region against growing evangelical competition. Throughout his visit, the US-born pope has also voiced strong criticism of Argentine President Javier Milei’s strict austerity policies. He argued that government spending cuts disproportionately harm the country’s poorest citizens. Difficult words: pontiff (the Pope, who acts as the chief bishop and leader of the Roman Catholic Church), pursuit (chasing or striving to achieve something), austerity (severity in government spending cutbacks and financial discipline).
